title: Syncretism and Its Critics
description: Where the word came from, who distrusts it, and two famous cases of gods combined and then pulled apart

concepts.title: A Word with a Checkered Past
concepts.contentHtml:
Syncretism, the combining of elements from different religions, is one of the oldest labels in the study of religion and one of the most disputed. The Greek synkretismos first appears in Plutarch's essay On Brotherly Love (about 100 CE), where it describes the Cretans, who quarreled among themselves but closed ranks against outside enemies. Erasmus revived the word in the early sixteenth century as praise for scholars who stood together despite their disagreements.

It turned sour in the seventeenth century. The Lutheran theologian Georg Calixtus (1586 to 1656) hoped to reconcile Lutherans, Calvinists and Catholics on a shared core of early Christian doctrine, and opponents such as Abraham Calov attacked his program as "syncretism": truth betrayed for the sake of peace. The word was also linked, probably wrongly, to the Greek verb synkerannymi, "to mix together," which helped fix its modern sense of blending. Christian missionaries later used it for converts who kept too much of their old religion.

Many scholars now stress that every tradition has mixed. Early Christianity absorbed Greek philosophy, and Buddhism took on local gods wherever it spread. In Syncretism/Anti-Syncretism (1994), the anthropologists Charles Stewart and Rosalind Shaw argued that the revealing question is who draws the boundaries. They used anti-syncretism for the work of reformers and officials who police religious borders and declare some mixtures impure. On this view "purity" is usually a claim made later about a mixed past, not an original condition. Some scholars drop the word for terms such as hybridity or creolization; others keep it as a neutral name for a process.

concepts.title: Serapis: A God for Two Peoples
concepts.contentHtml:
After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, his general Ptolemy took Egypt and came to rule from the new Greek city of Alexandria over Greek settlers and a far larger Egyptian population. The cult that came to bridge them was that of Serapis (earlier Sarapis). The name goes back to Egyptian Wsir-Hp, Osiris-Apis: at Memphis the sacred Apis bull was believed to merge with Osiris at death. Greeks in Memphis already prayed to this god before the Ptolemies; a fourth-century BCE Greek papyrus from Memphis addresses "Oserapis."

What changed under Ptolemy I (king from 305 to 282 BCE) was the god's look and reach. Serapis was shown as a bearded, enthroned Greek god resembling Zeus or Hades, with a grain measure (modius) on his head and the three-headed dog Cerberus at his feet, and he took on the roles of healer, giver of plenty and lord of the dead. Plutarch and Tacitus tell a founding story: Ptolemy dreamed of an unknown god, fetched a statue from Sinope on the Black Sea, and two advisers, Timotheus, an expert in the Eleusinian rites, and the Egyptian priest Manetho, identified it as Serapis. Most historians treat the Sinope tale as legend.

The cult won over Greeks more fully than Egyptians, many of whom kept worshiping Osiris and Apis in older forms. Serapis and Isis spread across the Mediterranean, to Delos, Rome and beyond, and Vespasian publicized healing miracles in Alexandria in 69 to 70 CE. The Alexandrian Serapeum, rebuilt on a grand scale under Ptolemy III, stood until 391 or 392 CE, when Christians led by Bishop Theophilus destroyed it.

concepts.title: Kami, Buddhas and the Separation of 1868
concepts.contentHtml:
When Buddhism reached Japan in the sixth century CE, it met the cults of the kami, deities of mountains, rivers, clans and places. For more than a thousand years the two were woven together in what scholars call shinbutsu-shūgō, the combination of kami and buddhas. Temples stood inside shrine precincts, monks performed rites for kami, and kami were said to seek Buddhist salvation like other beings. According to court chronicles, the god Hachiman pledged support for the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji in the 740s, and he came to be honored with the title of great bodhisattva (daibosatsu).

From the Heian period a theory called honji suijaku, "original ground and manifest trace," gave the mixture a logic: buddhas and bodhisattvas were the original forms, and kami were their local appearances. The sun goddess Amaterasu could be read as a manifestation of the cosmic Buddha Dainichi. In Nara, the Kasuga shrine and the Kōfuku-ji temple operated as one religious complex.

The new Meiji government ended this arrangement by decree. Orders issued from April 1868 required Buddhist images and titles to be removed from shrines and told monks who served shrines to become Shinto priests or leave; Hachiman could no longer be called a bodhisattva. The government did not explicitly order destruction, but a wave of attacks called haibutsu kishaku, "abolish Buddhism, destroy Shakyamuni," followed: thousands of temples closed, statues and scriptures were burned, and bells were melted down. In Satsuma domain every temple was shut. The historian Kuroda Toshio argued in 1981 that "Shinto" as a separate, self-contained religion is largely a modern creation, a purity built in the Meiji era and projected onto the past.

title: Cao Đài: The Third Era
description: A Vietnamese religion revealed through séances, with a Divine Eye, Victor Hugo as a saint, and an army

concepts.title: From Phú Quốc to Tây Ninh
concepts.contentHtml:
Cao Đài, formally Đại Đạo Tam Kỳ Phổ Độ, "the Great Way of the Third Era of Universal Salvation," was born in French-ruled southern Vietnam in the 1920s. Its first disciple, Ngô Văn Chiêu, was a colonial civil servant who took part in spirit séances. In 1921, while posted to Phú Quốc island, he reported a vision of a great left eye, which he took as the sign of the Supreme Being. That being was called Cao Đài, "High Tower" or "High Palace," a reverent title for God.

The religion took shape in Saigon in 1925, when a circle of young civil servants, among them Phạm Công Tắc, Cao Quỳnh Cư and Cao Hoài Sang, held séances with table-tapping and a basket fitted with a writing beak that traced characters. A spirit that first named itself only with the letters A Ă Â announced on Christmas Eve 1925 that it was Cao Đài, the Jade Emperor and the God of all religions. Lê Văn Trung, a former member of the colonial council, joined and brought organizing skill and money.

On 7 October 1926 a declaration announcing the new religion, signed by 28 leaders and 245 followers, went to the French governor of Cochinchina. In November 1926 a founding festival opened at the Gò Kén pagoda in Tây Ninh province, drawing crowds that reports put in the tens of thousands, and Lê Văn Trung became interim pope. Ngô Văn Chiêu declined leadership and founded a separate, meditative branch, the first of many splits. The movement spread fast among Mekong Delta peasants, partly because it offered a Vietnamese-led religion under colonial rule.

concepts.title: The Divine Eye and the Three Saints
concepts.contentHtml:
Every Cao Đài altar centers on the Divine Eye, a single left eye, often painted on a globe or in a triangle and surrounded by rays; Cao Đài writers explain the left side as yang, the side of the divine. The teaching divides history into three eras of salvation. In the first two, God sent founders such as the Buddha, Laozi, Confucius and Jesus, but their messages were distorted in human hands and divided humanity. In the Third Era God speaks directly, through spirit mediums, and unites all religions. Cao Đài honors five branches, the ways of humanity (Confucian ethics), of spirits, of saints (linked with Christianity), of immortals (Daoism) and of buddhas.

Séances were the engine of doctrine. Messages received by the mediums of the Hiệp Thiên Đài, the "Palace of Heavenly Union" led by Phạm Công Tắc, supplied laws, prayers and the appointment of clergy. The hierarchy borrows the shape of the Catholic Church, with a pope, cardinals, bishops and priests, and women may be ordained to all but the two highest ranks. The Holy See at Tây Ninh, built from the 1930s to the mid-1950s, combines pagoda roofs, cathedral towers and dragon-wrapped columns.

A mural in its entrance hall shows the Three Saints signing a "Third Alliance" between God and humanity: the French writer Victor Hugo, the Chinese revolutionary Sun Yat-sen holding an inkstone, and the sixteenth-century Vietnamese poet and seer Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm. Hugo writes "Dieu et Humanité, Amour et Justice." Hugo had held long table-turning séances in exile on Jersey from 1853 to 1855, and Cao Đài mediums received messages they attributed to him, naming him spiritual head of the overseas mission.

concepts.title: An Army, a Novel and a Long Recovery
concepts.contentHtml:
Cao Đài became a political force with an army of its own. French authorities, wary of a mass movement they could not control, closed temples and in 1941 exiled Phạm Công Tắc, by then its dominant leader, to an island prison off Madagascar. During the Japanese occupation, Cao Đài leaders such as Trần Quang Vinh organized armed units with Japanese backing, and in March 1945 Cao Đài militia helped the Japanese overthrow the French administration in the south.

After 1945 the Cao Đài, like the Hòa Hảo Buddhists and the Bình Xuyên crime syndicate, bargained with every side. Killings of members by the communist-led Việt Minh pushed the Tây Ninh leadership toward the French, with whom it allied after Tắc returned from exile in 1946. By the early 1950s its forces numbered in the tens of thousands by common estimates. One commander, Trình Minh Thế, broke away in 1951 to fight both the French and the communists, and his men claimed bombings in Saigon in 1952. Graham Greene drew on him for General Thé in The Quiet American (1955).

Ngô Đình Diệm, who took power in the south in 1954, broke the sect armies in 1955 and 1956. Thế rallied to Diệm and was killed in the Saigon fighting of 1955; Phạm Công Tắc fled to Cambodia and died there in 1959. After 1975 the communist government seized Cao Đài property and sent many members to re-education camps. The Tây Ninh Holy See regained legal recognition in 1997, under state-approved leadership that some overseas groups reject. Membership estimates range from about 2.5 million to more than 4 million, mostly in southern Vietnam.

title: Vodou: Serving the Spirits
description: African roots, Catholic saints, the Bois Caïman ceremony, and the gap between the religion and Hollywood 'voodoo'

concepts.title: Lwa, Saints and Servants
concepts.contentHtml:
Haitian Vodou took shape in the French colony of Saint-Domingue in the eighteenth century, among enslaved people taken from many parts of Africa. Its name comes from vodun, a Fon word for spirit or deity in what is now Benin. Fon, Yoruba and Kongo traditions all left their mark. Spirits are grouped into "nations" (nanchon): the cooler Rada, named for the West African kingdom of Allada, and the hot, forceful Petwo, with strong Kongo roots.

Vodouists speak of "serving the spirits." Above all stands Bondye (from French Bon Dieu), a creator too remote to address directly. Between Bondye and people are the lwa: Papa Legba, who opens the gate between worlds and is saluted first; Danbala, the serpent; Ezili, spirit of love in several forms; Ogou, the warrior; and the Gede spirits of death, led by Bawon Samedi. In ceremonies led by an oungan (priest) or manbo (priestess), with drums, songs and cornmeal designs called vèvè, a lwa may "mount" a devotee, who becomes its "horse" during possession.

Catholicism is woven in. The Code Noir of 1685 required that enslaved people be baptized, and many Kongolese arrived already Christian, since Kongo's kings had been Catholic since the 1490s. Lwa are linked to saints through popular prints: Danbala with Saint Patrick and his snakes, Legba with Saint Peter and his keys, Ogou with Saint James the Greater. An older theory held that saints were a mask to hide African gods from masters. Many scholars now argue that, whatever its origins, the pairing is sincere: many Vodouists consider themselves Catholics, and ceremonies often open with Catholic prayers.

concepts.title: Bois Caïman, 1791
concepts.contentHtml:
On the night of 22 to 23 August 1791, enslaved people on the sugar plantations of Saint-Domingue's Northern Plain rose in revolt. It was the start of the Haitian Revolution, which ended in independence in 1804. Haitian national memory places a Vodou ceremony at its origin. At Bois Caïman, a wooded spot near Le Cap, a gathering on a stormy night heard the oungan Dutty Boukman call for revolt; a priestess sacrificed a black pig, and the participants swore an oath of secrecy and vengeance.

The documentation is thin and late. Colonial records confirm that slave drivers and other leaders met on the Lenormand de Mézy plantation on 14 August 1791 to plan a rising. The pig sacrifice first appears in a history by Antoine Dalmas, a colonial doctor, published in 1814. Boukman's famous prayer, which sets the god of the whites, who demands crime, against the god who created the sun and wants vengeance, comes from Hérard Dumesle's travel account of 1824, based on testimony gathered decades later. The priestess's name, Cécile Fatiman, comes from later tradition, not from records of the time.

Historians divide over this. Léon-François Hoffmann argued in 1990 that the ceremony as told is largely a myth, assembled by later writers. David Geggus concluded that a religious ceremony probably did take place, perhaps a week after the 14 August meeting, and that the two events later merged in memory. Whatever happened, the story has been put to many uses. Haitian nationalists celebrate Bois Caïman as the founding act of the nation, while some evangelical preachers recast it as a pact with the devil, a reading Pat Robertson repeated after the 2010 earthquake.

concepts.title: Zombies, Dolls and Hollywood
concepts.contentHtml:
The English word "voodoo" carries a cargo of images that Vodou practitioners rarely recognize. Much of it was loaded during the United States occupation of Haiti from 1915 to 1934, when Marines and travel writers brought home lurid stories. William Seabrook's bestseller The Magic Island (1929) introduced American readers to the zombie, and the film White Zombie (1932), with Bela Lugosi as a sinister mill owner, set the template for decades of movies about drums, curses and the walking dead.

The realities differ. In Haitian folk belief a zonbi is a victim, a person whose soul or body has been seized by a sorcerer and put to work, a fear with obvious roots in slavery; it is not a flesh-eating monster. The ethnobotanist Wade Davis argued in The Serpent and the Rainbow (1985) that a powder containing pufferfish toxin could induce a deathlike state, but other scientists challenged his evidence, and the claim remains disputed. Pin-stuck "voodoo dolls" owe more to European image magic, New Orleans souvenir shops and film than to Haitian ritual. New Orleans has its own Voodoo tradition, associated with Marie Laveau (1801 to 1881).

Inside Haiti, Vodou faced repeated suppression. Campaigns against "superstition" backed by the Catholic hierarchy peaked in 1941 to 1942, when temples were raided and sacred objects burned. The 1987 constitution guaranteed freedom of religion, and in 2003 President Jean-Bertrand Aristide gave Vodou official recognition. Scholars and practitioners prefer the spelling "Vodou" partly to separate the religion from the Hollywood word.

title: Santería and Candomblé
description: Yoruba orishas in Cuba and Brazil, their Catholic doubles, and a 1993 Supreme Court case about animal sacrifice

concepts.title: Orishas in Cuba: Regla de Ocha
concepts.contentHtml:
The orishas (Yoruba òrìṣà) are the deities of the Yoruba-speaking peoples of what is now southwestern Nigeria and Benin. Each has its own domain, colors, foods and stories: Ṣàngó of thunder and kingship, Ògún of iron and war, Yemọja of the waters and motherhood, Ọ̀ṣun of rivers, love and wealth, Èṣù the messenger. In the early nineteenth century the wars that ended the Oyo empire sent large numbers of Yoruba captives into the Atlantic slave trade, especially to Cuba and to Bahia in Brazil.

In Cuba, where Yoruba people were called Lucumí and slave ships still landed until 1867, their religion survived partly through the cabildos de nación, mutual-aid societies for Africans of the same "nation," attached to Catholic parishes. The result is called Regla de Ocha ("rule of the orishas"), Lucumí, or Santería, "the way of the saints," a name once used dismissively by outsiders. Each oricha is paired with a Catholic saint or Virgin: Changó with Saint Barbara, patron of lightning, both dressed in red; Ochún with Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre, Cuba's patron; Yemayá with the Virgin of Regla; Babalú Ayé with Saint Lazarus; Obatalá with Our Lady of Mercy.

Initiation, called "making the saint" (kariocha), places an oricha on the initiate's head, and the new initiate, the iyawó, wears white for a year. Diviners read cowrie shells, and the babalawo, priest of Orula, practices Ifá divination. Offerings range from fruit to animals, most often birds, whose meat is usually cooked and eaten, except in rites of healing and death. Emigration after the 1959 revolution carried Santería to Miami, New York and beyond.

concepts.title: Candomblé in Bahia
concepts.contentHtml:
Brazil imported more enslaved Africans than any other country and abolished slavery only in 1888. There, in the nineteenth century, African religions regrouped as Candomblé, centered on the city of Salvador da Bahia. Its houses of worship (terreiros) belong to "nations" named for their African sources: Ketu or Nagô (Yoruba), Jeje (Fon and Ewe), and Angola (Central African, Bantu-speaking). The Yoruba-derived Ketu houses became the best known, and their deities, the orixás, carry Portuguese spellings: Xangô, Ogum, Iemanjá, Oxum, Oxalá.

Women have led Candomblé to a degree unusual among religions. Tradition traces the Casa Branca do Engenho Velho, regarded as the oldest Ketu terreiro, to African women in Salvador in the early nineteenth century, a founding story kept mainly in oral tradition. The American anthropologist Ruth Landes called Bahia The City of Women (1947), and the priestess Mãe Menininha do Gantois (1894 to 1986) became a national figure. In ceremonies, initiates dance until the orixás descend and possess them; the gods are then dressed in their colors and emblems.

Catholic devotion runs through the public calendar. Oxalá, father of the orixás, is linked with the Senhor do Bonfim (Lord of the Good End), and each January Bahian women in white wash the steps of the Bonfim church. Iemanjá, goddess of the sea, receives boats of flowers and gifts on 2 February. Terreiros faced police raids into the twentieth century, and in Bahia they had to register with the police until the 1970s. Some now face attacks by militant evangelicals, which activists call religious racism. Candomblé is distinct from Umbanda, a twentieth-century Brazilian religion that blends orixás with Spiritism.

concepts.title: Lukumi v. Hialeah, 1993
concepts.contentHtml:
In April 1987 the Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, a Santería congregation organized in Florida in 1973 and led by the priest Ernesto Pichardo, leased land in Hialeah, a city near Miami, and announced that it would practice openly, animal sacrifice included. The reaction was swift. At an emergency session in June 1987, council members and residents denounced the religion, and by September the city had passed ordinances banning the ritual killing of animals "not for the primary purpose of food consumption."

The ordinances were carefully drawn. They exempted kosher slaughter, licensed slaughterhouses, hunting, fishing, pest extermination and the euthanasia of strays, so almost the only killing they forbade was Santería sacrifice. The church sued, lost in the lower federal courts, and won at the Supreme Court. On 11 June 1993 the justices unanimously struck the ordinances down in Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah. Justice Anthony Kennedy's opinion held that the laws were neither neutral nor generally applicable: they had been "gerrymandered with care" to reach one religion's rite, so they faced strict scrutiny and failed it. "The Free Exercise Clause commits government itself to religious tolerance," he wrote.

The case is the essential companion to Employment Division v. Smith (1990), which held that neutral laws of general application may burden religious practice without special justification. Lukumi marked the limit: a law aimed at a religious practice is not neutral, however it is worded. The justices agreed on the result but split on the reasoning, and several used separate opinions to argue over whether Smith was right. For Santería, the ruling meant constitutional protection for a rite many neighbors found shocking.

title: Rastafari
description: From Garvey and a 1930 coronation to livity, reggae, and an emperor who never claimed to be God

concepts.title: A Black King Crowned
concepts.contentHtml:
Rastafari grew from older currents in Jamaican Black religion. "Ethiopianism," inspired by Psalm 68:31 ("Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God"), had long treated Ethiopia as a symbol of African dignity and ancient Christianity. The Jamaican activist Marcus Garvey (1887 to 1940), who founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in 1914, gave these hopes a mass audience with his call for Black self-reliance and a return to Africa. Rastas honor him as a prophet. A saying credited to him, "Look to Africa, when a black king shall be crowned," is widely quoted, but no contemporary source for it has been found.

On 2 November 1930, Ras Tafari Makonnen was crowned Emperor Haile Selassie I of Ethiopia, with titles that included King of Kings, Elect of God and Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah; his dynasty claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Jamaican newspapers covered the coronation, and several Kingston street preachers, above all Leonard Howell, began teaching that the emperor was the returned messiah of Revelation 5:5. The movement took its name from his earlier title: Ras, a high noble rank meaning "head," and his given name Tafari.

The colonial state saw sedition. Howell was convicted of sedition in 1934 and jailed for two years, partly for urging allegiance to Selassie rather than the British king. Around 1940 he founded Pinnacle, a commune in the hills of St Catherine, which police raided repeatedly until it was broken up in 1954. Garvey never embraced the movement. After Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935 and Selassie went into exile, Garvey attacked him in print, calling him a coward.

concepts.title: Livity: Ital, Locks and Reasoning
concepts.contentHtml:
Rastafari has no single church or creed. Its core is a way of life, called livity, and a set of shared themes: Haile Selassie, Jah, as God incarnate or God's chosen representative; Africa, and Ethiopia above all, as Zion; and the West and its institutions as Babylon, a system of oppression and exile. Rastas reshape English to fit this outlook, saying "I and I" for "we," or for the self united with God, and turning words such as "vital" into "ital."

Ital food is natural and unprocessed, often vegetarian or vegan and cooked without salt, and many Rastas avoid pork. Dreadlocks draw on the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, which forbids a razor on the head of one consecrated to God, and on the image of the lion's mane. Cannabis, called ganja or the holy herb, is treated as a sacrament during "reasonings," discussions of scripture and life, with verses such as Psalm 104:14 cited in support. Its use brought decades of arrests; Jamaica's 2015 drug-law reform decriminalized small amounts and allowed sacramental use by Rastafari.

The movement divided into "mansions." The Nyabinghi, the oldest strand, keeps drumming and chanting gatherings. The Bobo Shanti, founded by Prince Emmanuel Charles Edwards in 1958, wear turbans and keep a commune at Bull Bay. The Twelve Tribes of Israel, founded by Vernon Carrington in 1968, assign members to tribes by birth month. Reggae carried Rastafari worldwide in the 1970s, above all through Bob Marley (1945 to 1981), a Twelve Tribes member whose songs made Rasta language global. His "War" (1976) sets words from Selassie's 1963 speech to the United Nations.

concepts.title: The Emperor's Visit and the Emperor's Faith
concepts.contentHtml:
On 21 April 1966 Haile Selassie arrived in Kingston on a state visit. About 100,000 people, many of them Rastafari, crowded Palisadoes Airport on a stormy day and surged onto the tarmac, and the emperor stayed aboard his plane until the Rasta elder Mortimer Planno calmed the crowd. Rita Marley later said she saw the mark of a nail on his palm as he waved. Selassie received elders and gave them gold medallions, and he reportedly advised them not to move to Ethiopia before they had liberated Jamaica. Rastas mark 21 April as Grounation Day.

Selassie's own faith was Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity, which he practiced and promoted throughout his life. He did not claim to be divine. In a 1967 interview he said, "I told them clearly that I am a man, that I am mortal." Yet he never publicly rebuked the Rastafari, and he valued ties with the African diaspora. He had already granted land at Shashamane in southern Ethiopia for people of African descent from the West who wished to settle there, and by 1970 the Ethiopian Orthodox Church had a mission in Jamaica, where many Rastas were baptized.

The military regime called the Derg deposed him in 1974, and he died in its custody in August 1975; his remains were found only in 1992. Many Rastas refused to believe he had died, and Marley answered the news with the song "Jah Live." Marley himself, according to people close to him, was baptized into the Ethiopian Orthodox Church in late 1980 as Berhane Selassie, months before he died of cancer in May 1981. Rastafari never depended on the emperor's approval, and it has outlived both men.

title: Joke Religions and the Law
description: Discordians, Pastafarians and census Jedi, and what courts reveal when they decide what counts as a religion

concepts.title: Eris, Bob and the Noodly Appendage
concepts.contentHtml:
Parody religions borrow the forms of faith, such as scriptures, clergy, rituals and holidays, to make a point about them, and some followers come to treat them with real seriousness. Discordianism, the oldest of the modern kind, began in California in the late 1950s with two friends, Greg Hill and Kerry Thornley, who by Discordian lore received a vision of Eris, the Greek goddess of strife, in a bowling alley. Their scripture, the Principia Discordia, first printed in 1963, honors chaos, declares every man, woman and child a pope, and keeps readers unsure which jokes are serious. Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson's Illuminatus! trilogy (1975) carried it into the counterculture. The Church of the SubGenius, founded in Texas in the late 1970s around a grinning salesman called J. R. "Bob" Dobbs, satirized both religion and consumerism.

The most famous parody began with a letter. In January 2005 Bobby Henderson, a 24-year-old physics graduate, wrote to the Kansas State Board of Education, which was weighing whether science classes should present intelligent design alongside evolution. He demanded equal time for his own theory: that an invisible Flying Spaghetti Monster created the universe. After he posted the letter online in May 2005 it spread rapidly, and The Gospel of the Flying Spaghetti Monster followed in 2006.

Pastafarians, as followers call themselves, revere pirates and wear colanders. In 2011 Niko Alm in Austria won the right to wear a colander in his driving license photograph, a stunt aimed at religious exemptions in official rules. Others followed in the Czech Republic, Russia and elsewhere, and in April 2016 New Zealand saw its first legally recognized Pastafarian wedding.

concepts.title: The Jedi Census
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2001 the census of England and Wales asked about religion for the first time. Beforehand a chain email urged people to write "Jedi," claiming falsely that any faith with 10,000 adherents (8,000 in some versions) would win official recognition. On census day 390,127 people, almost 0.8 percent of the population, declared themselves Jedi, more than gave Judaism or Buddhism. Similar campaigns produced more than 70,000 Jedi in Australia, about 21,000 in Canada, and over 53,000 in New Zealand, about 1.5 percent of its people.

Statisticians handled the joke in different ways. The Office for National Statistics gave "Jedi Knight" its own code, 896, while stressing that this conferred no recognition. Many respondents were protesting the religion question itself, and the wave receded as the joke aged. England and Wales counted 176,632 Jedi in 2011; by 2021 the number had fallen below the threshold for publication, reportedly under 1,600.

A small number of people practice Jediism sincerely, as a philosophy of the Force drawn from the Star Wars films and from Daoist and Buddhist ideas. In December 2016 the Charity Commission for England and Wales refused charitable status to the Temple of the Jedi Order. It was not satisfied that Jediism involved belief in gods or in "spiritual or non-secular principles," found too little evidence that moral improvement was central to it, and described the group as essentially an online community. The commission was applying a definition from the UK Supreme Court's Scientology case, Hodkin (2013): a spiritual or non-secular belief system, held by a group, that claims to explain humanity's place in the universe and teaches followers how to live.

concepts.title: Courts and the Colander
concepts.contentHtml:
Courts in secular states face a bind. They may not decide whether a religion is true: in United States v. Ballard (1944) the US Supreme Court held that a jury could weigh whether believers sincerely held their beliefs, but not whether those beliefs were correct. Yet laws grant real privileges to religion, from tax exemptions to dress rules in prisons, so courts must still decide what counts. Parody religions are built to press on exactly that point.

In April 2016 a federal district court in Nebraska decided the case of Stephen Cavanaugh, a state prisoner who sought Pastafarian literature, clothing and worship. In Cavanaugh v. Bartelt, Judge John Gerrard ruled that the Flying Spaghetti Monster belief system is not a religion but "a parody, intended to advance an argument" about science and the place of religion in public schools. Reading its texts as scripture, he wrote, was an error of "basic reading comprehension." In the Netherlands, Mienke de Wilde asked to wear a colander in her passport and identity card photos. On 15 August 2018 the Council of State held that Pastafarianism is not a religion because it lacks the necessary seriousness and coherence, and in 2021 the European Court of Human Rights declared her complaint inadmissible, holding that Pastafarianism is not a "religion or belief" under Article 9.

These rulings show what legal definitions of religion lean on: seriousness, coherence, a group, and a moral or spiritual core, echoing the European test of views with "a certain level of cogency, seriousness, cohesion and importance." Those are exactly the features parody religions imitate. New Zealand, meanwhile, lets the same church conduct legal weddings.
